The operator, WCI, Inc., sued the Ohio Liquor Control Commission and Department of Public Safety to recover a $25,000 fine it paid under protest after state officials treated a dancer's nudity as a liquor permit violation.

The Ohio Liquor Control Commission revoked the liquor permit effective Sept. 20, 2018, after an Ohio Investigative Unit investigation in which agents bought drugs and lap dances with food stamp benefits.
The Montgomery County Prosecutor announced the club had been shut down after the prosecutor's office sought a preliminary injunction; 11 people faced sex, drug and food stamp charges.
Lost its liquor license in May 2018.
Raided in 2017. The Ohio State Highway Patrol said it was charged, along with The Harem and Sharkey's, in an administrative case before the Ohio Liquor Control Commission.
The Ohio Division of Liquor Control rejected the operator's liquor permit renewal, finding it had operated in disregard of state laws and local ordinances. The decision was appealable.
A homicide occurred in the club's parking lot in 2017, per WHIO.
Described as closed in January 2020 news coverage.
WTOL reported the club is named in a civil lawsuit and in two criminal cases arising from two drunk-driving crashes that killed three people.
Akron City Council unanimously passed a resolution objecting to renewal of the club's liquor permit after dozens of police calls; the city prosecutor also objected. Year to confirm.
Listed (as X Gentleman's club) on the Columbus City Attorney's liquor permit objection list sent to City Council for a vote. Date to confirm.

In Hart v. Rick's Cabaret, a federal judge in New York awarded about $10.9 million to a class of dancers after finding the club had misclassified them as independent contractors. History (older than 5 years).

A federal jury convicted the club's owner of sex trafficking conspiracy, bribery of a DEA agent, maintaining a drug-involved premises, narcotics conspiracy, witness tampering and cocaine distribution. Prosecutors said drugs and coercion were used to force dancers into sex acts inside the club.
The owner was sentenced to 25 years in federal prison.
Closed after its temporary liquor license expired following the owner's convictions.

In Dancer plaintiffs v. Shanlee, Inc. d/b/a Fantasia Gentlemen's Club, the court conditionally certified an FLSA collective; dancers allege no wages, a $50 per-shift tip-out, jukebox fees, $40-$100 lateness fines and a club share of private-dance payments. Employee status not yet decided.

Named among defendants in Dancer plaintiffs v. SFBSC Management, LLC et al., a misclassification and tip-sharing class and collective action; the court gave final approval to a settlement of at least $6.5 million ($4M cash, $500K dance-fee pool, changed practices) for 8,402 dancers at San Francisco and other California clubs.

California's Department of Fair Employment and Housing announced a $260,000 settlement resolving allegations that a manager coerced dancers under their supervision into sex acts and that management and patrons sexually harassed and assaulted dancers; terms include an anti-harassment policy, training and three years of state monitoring.

The NLRB docket shows a bilateral settlement agreement in the dancers' retaliation case; per Actors' Equity, the owners withdrew election challenges, agreed to recognize the union and bargain, and agreed to reopen and bring back dancers dismissed in 2022.

The NLRB General Counsel issued a complaint in March 2024 alleging the club breached its 2023 settlement with dancers; on July 17, 2024 the Board denied a default judgment, finding a factual dispute over compliance, and remanded the case to the Regional Director.

A bouncer at the club, described as primarily responsible for hiring dancers, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to use an interstate facility to promote or facilitate prostitution, per Homeland Security Investigations.

The club's former owner, who pleaded guilty in May 2026 to conspiracy to use an interstate facility to promote prostitution plus tax-fraud and money-laundering counts, was sentenced to 16 months in federal prison and ordered to pay $549,999 to the IRS and $150,000 to the SBA, per IRS-CI. The release says the owner and employees promoted and facilitated prostitution in the club's private rooms.

Named in an FLSA suit by three former dancers alleging misclassification as independent contractors and unpaid minimum wage; the court denied conditional certification without prejudice because no other dancers had shown interest in joining.

The court held the dancers were employees under the FLSA and Florida Minimum Wage Act, rejecting the operators' licensee argument and their offset, unjust enrichment and breach-of-contract counterclaims; overtime claims of named plaintiffs failed for lack of hours over 40.

The court held the dancers were employees under the FLSA and Florida Minimum Wage Act, rejecting the operators' licensee argument and their offset, unjust enrichment and breach-of-contract counterclaims; overtime claims of named plaintiffs failed for lack of hours over 40.

In Dancer plaintiff v. Emperor's Tampa, Inc. et al., the court held as a matter of law that the dancer was an FLSA employee and the clubs' owner an employer; coverage, willfulness and wage offsets were left for trial. The dancer alleges unpaid minimum wage, stage fees and kickbacks.

In Dancer plaintiff v. Emperor's Tampa, Inc. et al., the court held as a matter of law that the dancer was an FLSA employee and the clubs' owner an employer; coverage, willfulness and wage offsets were left for trial. The dancer alleges unpaid minimum wage, stage fees and kickbacks.

In Dancer plaintiffs v. Entertainment 2851 LLC et al., the court conditionally certified an FLSA collective of dancers alleging misclassification, unpaid minimum and overtime wages, house fees and required tip pooling with security and floor staff; defendants deny the allegations.

The Florida Attorney General's Office of Statewide Prosecution announced the club's owner was convicted of racketeering, conspiracy, cocaine trafficking and money laundering after a Tampa Police undercover probe into drug sales and human trafficking at the club, where officers said they were offered commercial sex. The listed convictions do not include a human trafficking count.

In Dancer plaintiff v. Miami Gardens Square One, Inc. d/b/a Tootsie's Cabaret Miami, the court granted summary judgment in part and denied it in part, finding a genuine dispute over whether the dancer was an employee; testimony described a house fee, a $5 per-dance club share and tip-outs to staff.

In Dancer plaintiff v. WBY, Inc. d/b/a The Follies, the court granted partial summary judgment holding the dancer was an FLSA employee, not an independent contractor, and that the club violated minimum wage law by paying no wages; damages were left for trial.

The club settled an EEOC Title VII suit for $200,000 under a consent decree; the EEOC alleged entertainers faced sexual harassment and physical assaults by customers, that Black entertainers faced particular abuse, and that a complaining entertainer was not called back. The decree requires training, a deny-entry list for customers with repeated harassment complaints, and discipline for security staff who fail to act.

In Dancer plaintiff v. Marshall International, LLC d/b/a Gold Club Chicago, the court conditionally certified an FLSA collective of dancers alleging misclassification, no wages and per-shift house fees; three dancers with one arbitration agreement version were excluded from notice.

In Dancer plaintiff v. CSWS, LLC d/b/a Ocean's Gentlemen's Club, the court conditionally certified an FLSA collective; dancers allege no wages, a $50 house fee plus per-shift payments to management, house parent, DJ and security, and fines of $20 to $500.

In Dancer plaintiffs v. Clinton Entertainment Management, LLC d/b/a The Pink Monkey, the court granted the club summary judgment on FLSA minimum wage and tip claims, holding dance fees were service charges and weekly pay exceeded the minimum; employee status was not decided and state claims were dismissed without prejudice.

US Department of Labor sued the club and its operator on behalf of 80 dancers, alleging misclassification as independent contractors, unlawful fees taken from tips, unpaid wages and contracts requiring dancers to repay recovered wages; seeks back wages and equal liquidated damages.

The court entered default judgment for a former dancer against Bottoms Up Gentlemen's Club, LLC and Chez Joey, LLC as joint employers under the FLSA and Maryland law, awarding $86,932.23 in unpaid wages and retained tips and fees plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, fees and costs.

The court entered default judgment for a former dancer against Chez Joey, LLC and Bottoms Up Gentlemen's Club, LLC as joint employers under the FLSA and Maryland law, awarding $86,932.23 in unpaid wages and retained tips and fees plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, fees and costs.

In Dancer plaintiff v. PP&G, Inc. d/b/a Norma Jeans Gentlemen's Club, the court conditionally certified an FLSA collective; the dancer alleges no wages, a $45-$100 per-shift house fee and $40-$100 per shift in tips paid to managers and others.

Dancer plaintiffs v. The Coliseum, Inc. et al. alleges dancers were misclassified as independent contractors, denied minimum wage and required to pay tip kickbacks to managers, bouncers, DJs and house mothers; the court denied initial notice without prejudice, ordered expedited discovery and tolled limitations.

Named as a defendant in an FLSA and Nebraska Wage and Hour Act suit alleging dancers were misclassified, paid no minimum wage, and charged house fees, late fees, fines and mandatory DJ tip-outs. A magistrate judge recommended denying dismissal and conditionally certifying a collective.

A dancer sued under the FLSA and New Jersey wage laws alleging misclassification; the Third Circuit reversed an order sending the claims to arbitration, holding the club's dancer rental agreement did not cover statutory wage claims.

Named as a defendant in an FLSA and New Jersey wage suit alleging dancers were paid no wages and charged a fixed per-shift house fee and DJ fee and required to share tips. The court conditionally certified a collective and certified a state-law class.

The Nevada Supreme Court reversed summary judgment for the club, holding that dancers were employees under the economic realities test for purposes of Nevada's constitutional minimum wage and that the statutory independent-contractor presumption cannot override it. Remanded.

The federal court granted dancers partial summary judgment, finding they were employees under the FLSA and that the club failed to pay minimum and overtime wages; the record describes per-shift house, marketing and DJ fees and a 10% cut of dance-dollar payments. Willfulness and damages were left for trial.

A dancer sued under the FLSA and New York Labor Law alleging employee status; the record describes pay solely from tips and a nightly fee of at least $10 paid to the house mom. The court denied the club's summary judgment motion and sent employee status to trial.
The court granted two dancers summary judgment on federal and Ohio minimum-wage claims, finding they were employees and the owner jointly liable, and awarded about $17,745 and $17,191.

The Columbus City Attorney obtained an emergency court order closing the property as a criminal nuisance, saying a lingerie store fronted an unlicensed strip club where a July 2019 shootout wounded two people and police made covert cocaine buys.

Named as a defendant in an FLSA and Oklahoma Minimum Wage Act suit alleging dancers were paid no wages, charged house, bar and DJ fees, and required to share tips with non-tipped staff. The court denied the owner's motion to dismiss.
Named as a defendant in an FLSA suit challenging the classification of dancers as independent contractors; the court conditionally certified a collective of dancers from 2013 onward.

Dancers voted 16-0 for Actors' Equity Association representation, and the NLRB certified the union as their bargaining representative on Sept. 15, 2023; dancers had struck since April 2023 over safety conditions.
On default, the NLRB found the club violated the National Labor Relations Act by failing and refusing to bargain in good faith with Actors' Equity, the dancers' certified union.

On default (no answer filed), the NLRB found the club unlawfully fired a dancer for raising safety concerns, threatened workers over criticizing the company, and that the majority owner and an employee threw picket signs, pushed picketers and set off fireworks toward them during a strike; it ordered reinstatement with backpay.

Named as a defendant in a dancer's FLSA misclassification and retaliation suit; the Ninth Circuit reversed summary judgment for the defendants on the retaliation claim and remanded for a decision on whether the dancer was an employee. The underlying federal wage claims were held untimely.

A dancer sued under the FLSA alleging no wages, mandatory house fees, tip-outs of 15 to 20 percent and private-room fees. A magistrate judge recommended finding the dancer was an employee, that violations were willful, and denying the club's summary judgment motion.

The operator of the striptease club and an adjoining brothel, convicted by a jury in 2016 of sex trafficking by force, was sentenced to 100 years in federal prison; prosecutors said the operator and three co-defendants used force, threats, fraud and coercion against young women, per the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

The Third Circuit affirmed a jury verdict of more than $4.5 million for a class of dancers on Pennsylvania minimum-wage and unjust-enrichment claims, and upheld the ruling that the dancers were employees, not independent contractors.

Named as a defendant in an FLSA and Pennsylvania wage suit alleging mandatory deductions from dancers' tips, including a house fee of about 15% of tips, per-staff tip-outs, late fees and short-shift fees. The court conditionally certified a collective.

Named as a defendant in an FLSA and Pennsylvania wage suit alleging dancers were misclassified, unpaid, and had tips taken for business expenses. The court conditionally certified a collective and certified a state-law class for work through January 24, 2016, including successor-liability claims against the later owner.

The court approved a $1.5 million class settlement for dancers who worked at the club from December 4, 2010 to February 7, 2019, in an FLSA and state wage suit alleging misclassification. Not an admission of liability.

The Knox County District Attorney announced a judge ordered the club closed under the state nuisance law after a homicide, repeated shootings, fights and more than 80 police calls for service; the petition said owners and managers were unwilling or unable to control criminal activity.

On an unopposed summary judgment motion, the court found a dancer was an employee, not an independent contractor, and entered judgment of $88,425 for unpaid minimum wage, $20-per-shift house fee reimbursement and liquidated damages.

Named as a defendant in an FLSA suit alleging dancers were misclassified, paid no wages, and charged a $50 license fee and rent; the court denied dancers' motion for partial summary judgment, finding factual disputes on employee status.

Dancers sued under the FLSA alleging misclassification; in this order the court granted the club partial summary judgment on overtime and off-the-clock claims and dismissed one individual defendant. Employee status was not decided in this order.

Ten dancers sued under the FLSA alleging misclassification, no wages, mandatory house fees, early-leave fees and required tip-sharing; the court left employee status for trial and struck several of the club's affirmative defenses.

Three men were sentenced (210, 120 and 34 months) after pleading guilty in a scheme in which women smuggled from Cuba were given debts of up to $30,000 and made to dance and perform commercial sex at Houston-area clubs, including this one, per the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas.

The U.S. Attorney for the Virgin Islands announced a federal criminal complaint charging the club's owner, a manager and a driver with conspiracy to transport for prostitution, travel in aid of racketeering, and harboring aliens for financial gain, alleging the club was run as a brothel with a coercive fee scheme. Charges are allegations; defendants are presumed innocent.

A federal grand jury indicted the club's owner and a former manager for conspiracy to use interstate facilities to promote prostitution; the owner was also charged with filing false tax returns for 2015 and 2016, per the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Wisconsin.

A federal grand jury indicted an owner and a former bartender/manager for conspiring from 2009 to 2018 to use interstate facilities to promote prostitution at the club; the owner was also charged with lying to agents investigating human trafficking, per the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Wisconsin.

After a June 23, 2026 hearing, the Connecticut Liquor Control Commission ordered the club's cafe liquor permit revoked, effective immediately, finding nine violations (four counts each under Regs. Conn. State Agencies 30-6-A24(b) and (c), and one under Conn. Gen. Stat. 30-47(a)(6)). The findings rest on a March 27-28, 2026 joint investigation with State Police in which dancers exposed themselves and mingled with patrons, including lap dances in the bar area; the Commission found it not credible that this was isolated and found the permittee lacked control of daily operations.

The U.S. Attorney for the District of Kansas announced that a man who began working at Club Magic, a Lawrence nightclub, in 2012 for the organization's leader pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to operate an interstate sex trafficking business; he admitted transporting people working as prostitutes to client meetings and advertising them online. The organization's leader was awaiting trial.

Named as a defendant, with ACT Distributors and GPT (DE) LLC, in an FLSA suit by a former dancer (later four dancers) alleging misclassification as independent contractors and unpaid minimum wage, that dancers were encouraged to tip DJs, managers and security staff, that the club kept private-dance fees, and that dancers paid a house fee each shift. In a November 22, 2022 order the court declined to approve proposed individual settlements totaling $70,000.60 ($37,913.70 net to the dancers), citing an unexplained low share for one dancer and unsupported fees. Allegations, not findings.

Named as a defendant, with three RCI entities, in a collective action in federal court in Manhattan that Bloomberg Law reported alleges more than 100 dancers were misclassified as independent contractors and deprived of about $2 million in wages and tips. The court's December 2025 judgment (Doc. 198) confirms the parties and docket: it entered $5,000, including fees and costs, for one plaintiff who accepted the defendants' Rule 68 offer of judgment, jointly against the club entity, the RCI entities and two individual defendants. Allegations otherwise not decided.

The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment that two former dancers at The Brass Pole in Elyria were employees, not independent contractors, under the FLSA, leaving in place minimum-wage awards of $17,744.97 and $17,191.26.

Named as a defendant in Doe 1 et al. v. VM3015, Inc. et al., in which dancers allege Ohio clubs and the Buckeye Association of Club Executives (BACE) misclassified dancers as independent contractors and paid no wages, and conspired to do so through 'tenant' lease agreements. A March 4, 2019 order stayed the conspiracy claims pending certification in a related case and let individual-club wage claims proceed. Allegations, not findings.

The court approved the parties' FLSA settlement agreement (Order Approving Settlement Agreement, Doc. 198), finding it fair, reasonable and adequate, in a suit alleging dancers at Gold Cup, Cover Girls, Treasures and Centerfolds were misclassified as independent contractors and not paid as the FLSA requires. The order states no amount; news reported $1.1 million, about $579,700 to dancers. A settlement is not an admission of liability.

The 151st District Court of Harris County issued an ex parte temporary restraining order barring the club from operating any sexually oriented business at 7004 Charles Road without the required Harris County permit, finding it was operating without one, that performers had agreed to and been charged with prostitution, and that the defendants had not made reasonable efforts to abate it. The order was posted by the Harris County Attorney's Office.

Tarrant County announced that the State of Texas filed a public nuisance lawsuit against the club on May 30, 2023, to be handled by the Tarrant County Criminal District Attorney's office, and that the county administrator had opened an inquiry into revoking the club's sexually oriented business permit because it is within 1,000 feet of residences, with a county board hearing set for June 21, 2023. CBS Texas reported the suit followed a shooting that left one dead and three injured and cited more than 200 calls for service from 2020 to 2022; the county release does not mention these.

The order states no amount; news reported $1.1 million, about $579,700 to dancers. A settlement is not an admission of liability.

The Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection issued a notice of charges seeking revocation or suspension of the club's liquor permit, citing a May 14, 2024 federal indictment of the club's owner/controller, manager and a bouncer for conspiring to facilitate prostitution at the premises from about January 2020 to March 2023, and June 21-22, 2024 inspections in which agents saw dancers expose themselves and mingle with patrons. Charges, not findings.

The Providence Board of Licenses agenda for November 1, 2018 lists the club's operator under 'To appear show cause' regarding an incident of June 24, 2018. The agenda does not describe the incident or the outcome.

The Rhode Island Department of Business Regulation's liquor enforcement index lists an appeal by the club's operator against a Providence licensing action, with a decision on its motion for stay (Dec. 24, 2018), second and third orders on the stay (Jan. 4 and 8, 2019) and an order of dismissal (June 12, 2019). The index does not say what the Board did or why.
